blocks.text: The praise in verses 1–7 moves through animals, architecture, agriculture, and landscape. These comparisons make the lover’s admiring gaze and imaginative description central to the poem, rather than presenting a literal inventory of the woman’s body.

Jewish readings of the Song as portraying God and Israel, and Christian readings involving Christ and the church or the Word and the soul, are major theological traditions. The Song itself uses recurring images and phrases to create poetic coherence, but its sequence does not establish one uncontested plot, wedding cycle, dream sequence, or biography. These traditions should therefore be recognized as readings of the poetry rather than explicit identifications made by its speakers.
